facts.fact_text: On 19 July 1989 the applicant joined an anti-Turkish demonstration in the Ayios Kassianos area in Nicosia.
According to an affidavit sworn by the applicant before the Nicosia District Court on 3 January 2000, the demonstration of 19 July 1989 was peaceful.

According to an affidavit sworn by the applicant before the Nicosia District Court on 3 January 2000, the demonstration of 19 July 1989 was held on the fifteenth anniversary of the Turkish intervention in Cyprus.

According to an affidavit sworn by the applicant before the Nicosia District Court on 3 January 2000, the demonstration of 19 July 1989 was held in support of missing persons and to protest against human rights violations.

After United Nations soldiers had shouted a warning to the demonstrators not to advance further, the applicant was seized by the hair by Turkish military personnel and/or other personnel acting under Turkish control.
The applicant was beaten and assaulted by Turkish military personnel and/or other personnel acting under Turkish control.
The applicant was dragged to a small, stiflingly hot room in which other demonstrators were also being held.
Later on 20 July 1989, after being subjected to a body search, the applicant was taken to a court which remanded her in custody for two days.
The applicant was transferred with other women who had been arrested at the same time to the Ortakeuy prison.

On 22 July 1989, the Nicosia District Court ordered the applicant to enter into a recognizance of 1,000,000 Turkish liras as a guarantee that she would not commit further breaches of the peace for a period of one year.

Most of the accused, including the applicant, were sentenced to 2 days' imprisonment and a fine of 50 Cypriot pounds (approximately 85 euros), with five additional days in prison in default of payment within 24 hours.
After the public delivery of the judgment on 22 July 1989, the accused, including the applicant, were returned to prison.

The English translation of the Nicosia District Court judgment of 22 July 1989 indicates that the applicant, together with 23 other women, was charged with entering 'TRNC' territory without permission, contrary to sections 2, 8 and 9 of Law No. 5/72.

The English translation of the Nicosia District Court judgment of 22 July 1989 indicates that the applicant, together with 23 other women, was charged with entering 'TRNC' territory other than through an approved port, contrary to subsections 12(1) and (5) of the Aliens and Immigration Law.

Section 9 of Law No. 5/72 states that any person who enters a prohibited military area without authorization, or by stealth, or fraudulently, shall be tried by a military court in accordance with the Military Offences Act, and those found guilty shall be punished.
Subsection 12(1) of the Aliens and Immigration Law states that no person shall enter or leave the Colony except through an approved port.

Subsection 12(5) of the Aliens and Immigration Law states that any person who contravenes or fails to observe any of the provisions of subsections (1), (2), (3) or (4) of section 12 shall be guilty of an offence and shall be liable to imprisonment for a term not exceeding six months or to a fine not exceeding one hundred pounds or to both such imprisonment and fine.
The Government alleged that the applicant had participated in a violent demonstration with the aim of enflaming anti-Turkish sentiment.
The Government alleged that the demonstrators, supported by the Greek-Cypriot administration, were demanding that the 'Green Line' in Nicosia should be dismantled.
The Government alleged that the demonstrators were warned in Greek and English that unless they dispersed they would be arrested in accordance with the laws of the 'TRNC'.

The Government alleged that the Turkish-Cypriot police intervened in the face of the manifest inability of the Greek-Cypriot authorities and the UN Force in Cyprus to contain the incursion and its possible consequences.
In his report of 7 December 1989 on UN operations in Cyprus, the UN Secretary General stated that a serious situation arose in July 1989 as a result of a demonstration by Greek Cypriots in Nicosia.

The UN Secretary General stated that in the evening of 19 July 1989, some 1,000 Greek Cypriot demonstrators, mostly women, forced their way into the UN buffer zone in the Ayios Kassianos area of Nicosia.

The UN Secretary General stated that on 21 July 1989, he expressed his concern at the events that had taken place and stressed that it was vital that all parties keep in mind the purpose of the UN buffer zone as well as their responsibility to ensure that that area was not violated.

The UN Secretary General stated that on 24 July 1989, the President of the Security Council announced that he had conveyed to the representatives of all the parties, on behalf of the members of the Council, the Council's deep concern at the tense situation created by the incidents of 19 July 1989.
According to an affidavit sworn by the applicant before the Nicosia District Court on 3 January 2000, the demonstration of 19 July 1989 was peaceful.
United Nations soldiers shouted a warning to the demonstrators not to advance further.

After United Nations soldiers had shouted a warning to the demonstrators not to advance further, the applicant was seized by the hair by Turkish military personnel and/or other personnel acting under Turkish control.
The applicant was beaten and assaulted by Turkish military personnel and/or other personnel acting under Turkish control.
The beating of the applicant was inflicted with electrical batons by 3 or 4 policemen all over the applicant's body, in particular the head and back.
One of the blows to the applicant caused a painful injury to the applicant's right arm and elbow, with loss of blood.
The applicant was dragged to a small, stiflingly hot room in which other demonstrators were also being held.
One of the prisoners in the small room where the applicant was held had been severely beaten and was unconscious.
The applicant and the other detainees were led through a hostile crowd that spat and swore at them to a bus waiting to take them to the so-called 'Pavlides Garage'.
As the applicant entered the Pavlides Garage, her handbag was seized.
The applicant was forced to sit on the floor at the Pavlides Garage.
The toilet facilities at the Pavlides Garage were filthy.
A crowd gathered outside the Pavlides Garage was swearing, shouting abuse and threats, and throwing stones, some of which came through the corrugated iron roof.
One of the detainees at the Pavlides Garage, a doctor, treated the applicant's arm, which was still bleeding, with whatever he had to hand and bandaged it.
One of the female prisoners, Mrs Vrahimi (application no. 16078/90), was beaten in front of the other detainees at the Pavlides Garage.
The other detainees at the Pavlides Garage remained silent while Mrs Vrahimi was beaten, fearing for their own fate.
A woman at the Pavlides Garage shouted that she was an American citizen and was released shortly afterwards.
While in the Pavlides Garage, the applicant was interrogated.
The applicant refused to sign the statement produced during interrogation at the Pavlides Garage, which was written in Turkish.
The interrogation at the Pavlides Garage took place in Greek and touched mainly on political subjects.
On 20 July 1989, the applicant and the other detainees were photographed and filmed by a television crew.
Later on 20 July 1989, after being subjected to a body search, the applicant was taken to a court which remanded her in custody for two days.
The applicant was transferred with other women who had been arrested at the same time to the Ortakeuy prison.
At the Ortakeuy prison, the applicant was held in a cell with another woman.
The conditions of detention at the Ortakeuy prison were appalling and the cell was unbearably hot.
During the night at the Ortakeuy prison, the applicant and the other detainees were constantly checked and counted by the guards and as a result were unable to sleep.
The applicant went on hunger strike while detained at the Ortakeuy prison.
During the evening of 21 July 1989, the applicant was taken to the Nicosia District Court for trial.
The judge at the Nicosia District Court asked the applicant and the other accused whether they wanted legal representation.
The applicant and the other accused replied that they would only accept as defence counsel a lawyer registered with the bar association of the Republic of Cyprus.
As a result of the applicant and the other accused refusing to accept a lawyer not registered with the bar association of the Republic of Cyprus, they were not assisted by a lawyer at trial.
The interpretation into Greek at the Nicosia District Court trial was poor and did not cover all the words used by the witnesses and the parties.
Each time an accused tried to speak and give an explanation at the Nicosia District Court trial, she was interrupted.

Although the applicant had never previously seen some of the exhibits produced at the trial, notably a pair of scissors, gloves and a saw, one of the prosecution witnesses said that he had found a penknife in the applicant's handbag.
The applicant alleged that she had taken the penknife with her to peel an apple and that the blade was not even two inches long.
The applicant tried to explain her position regarding the penknife to the judge but was not allowed to.
The applicant showed her bandaged arm in order to complain about the beating she had suffered, but an officer replied that she could have injured herself by falling down.
After the trial at the Nicosia District Court, the applicant was taken back to prison.

On 22 July 1989, the Nicosia District Court ordered the applicant to enter into a recognizance of 1,000,000 Turkish liras as a guarantee that she would not commit further breaches of the peace for a period of one year.
The trial judge at the Nicosia District Court noted that it was the second time the applicant had illegally entered 'TRNC' territory.

Most of the accused, including the applicant, were sentenced to 2 days' imprisonment and a fine of 50 Cypriot pounds (approximately 85 euros), with five additional days in prison in default of payment within 24 hours.
After the public delivery of the judgment on 22 July 1989, the accused, including the applicant, were returned to prison.
On 24 July 1989, the applicant was released and taken by bus to southern Cyprus.
As a result of the beating described in the applicant's account, three of the applicant's vertebrae were damaged.
Doctors told the applicant that the condition of her central nerve was continuously deteriorating and that no surgery could be carried out.
The Government alleged that some demonstrators carried Greek flags, clubs, knives and wire-cutters.
The Government alleged that the demonstrators were acting in a provocative manner and shouting abuse.
The Government alleged that the applicant was arrested by the Turkish-Cypriot police after crossing the UN buffer zone and entering the area under Turkish-Cypriot control.
The Government alleged that no force was used against demonstrators who did not intrude into the 'TRNC' border area.

The Government alleged that in the case of demonstrators who were arrested for violating the border, no more force was used than was reasonably necessary in the circumstances in order to arrest and detain the persons concerned.
The Government alleged that no one was ill-treated.
The Government alleged that it was possible that some of the demonstrators had hurt themselves in the confusion or in attempting to scale barbed wire or other fencing.

The Government alleged that had the Turkish police, or anyone else, assaulted or beaten any of the demonstrators, the UN Secretary General would no doubt have referred to this in his report to the Security Council.
The Government alleged that the applicant was charged, tried, found guilty and sentenced to a short term of imprisonment.
The Government alleged that the applicant pleaded not guilty but did not give evidence and declined to use the available judicial remedies.
The Government alleged that the applicant was asked if she required assistance from a lawyer registered in the 'TRNC', but refused and did not ask for legal representation.
The Government alleged that interpretation services were provided at the trial by qualified interpreters and that all the proceedings were translated into Greek.
The UN Secretary General stated that the demonstrators broke through a wire barrier maintained by the United Nations Force in Cyprus (UNFICYP) and destroyed an UNFICYP observation post.

The UN Secretary General stated that the demonstrators broke through the line formed by UNFICYP soldiers and entered a former school complex where UNFICYP reinforcements regrouped to prevent them from proceeding further.
The UN Secretary General stated that a short while later, Turkish-Cypriot police and security forces elements forced their way into the area and apprehended 111 persons, 101 of them women.
The UN Secretary General stated that the Ayios Kassianos school complex is situated in the UN buffer zone, but that the Turkish forces claim it to be on their side of the cease-fire line.

The UN Secretary General stated that under working arrangements with UNFICYP, the Turkish-Cypriot security forces had patrolled the Ayios Kassianos school grounds for several years within specific restrictions, and that this patrolling had ceased altogether as part of an unmanning agreement implemented in May 1989.

The UN Secretary General stated that in the afternoon of 21 July 1989, some 300 Greek Cypriots gathered at the main entrance to the UN protected area in Nicosia, where the UN headquarters is located, to protest the continuing detention by the Turkish-Cypriot authorities of those apprehended at Ayios Kassianos.

The UN Secretary General stated that the number of demonstrators at the UN protected area entrance fluctuated between 200 and 2,000, and that they blocked all UN traffic through the entrance until 30 July 1989, when the Turkish-Cypriot authorities released the last two detainees.

The UN Secretary General stated that the events of 19 July 1989 created considerable tension in Cyprus and that intensive efforts were made, both at the UN headquarters and at Nicosia, to contain and resolve the situation.
The UN Secretary General stated that on 21 July 1989, he urged the Turkish-Cypriot authorities to release without delay all those who had been detained.

The UN Secretary General stated that the President of the Security Council stressed the need strictly to respect the UN buffer zone and appealed for the immediate release of all persons still detained.

The UN Secretary General stated that the President of the Security Council asked all concerned to show maximum restraint and to take urgent steps that would bring about a relaxation of tension and contribute to the creation of an atmosphere favourable to the negotiations.
The applicant produced 21 photographs taken at different times during the demonstration on 19 July 1989.
Photographs 1 to 7 produced by the applicant were intended to show that, notwithstanding the deployment of the Turkish-Cypriot police, the demonstration of 19 July 1989 was peaceful.
In photographs 8 to 10 produced by the applicant, members of the Turkish-Cypriot police are seen breaking up the UNFICYP cordon.
The final set of photographs produced by the applicant show members of the Turkish-Cypriot police using force to arrest some of the women demonstrators.
The Nicosia District Court judgment of 22 July 1989 was given in the presence of the accused and of an interpreter.

The trial judge at the Nicosia District Court noted that the accused did not accept the charges against them and stated that they did not wish to use the services of a lawyer registered in the 'TRNC'.
The trial judge at the Nicosia District Court noted that some of the accused had fainted during the trial and had been taken to hospital and excused from attending the hearing.
The trial judge at the Nicosia District Court noted that the public prosecutor called 7 witnesses, whose statements were translated into Greek for the accused's benefit.

The trial judge at the Nicosia District Court noted that the witnesses, mainly police officers on duty at the time of the demonstration, declared that the accused had illegally entered the 'TRNC' buffer zone, shouted abuse at the Turkish-Cypriot forces, and resisted arrest by pulling and pushing.
The trial judge at the Nicosia District Court noted that knives and other cutting objects had been found in the bags of some of the demonstrators who had been arrested.

The trial judge at the Nicosia District Court noted that witnesses declared that the demonstrators had passed the barriers at the UN observation post, broken the wooden door of a church and moved toward a water reservoir.
The trial judge at the Nicosia District Court noted that according to a map shown at trial, the area where the accused had entered was 'TRNC' territory.
The trial judge at the Nicosia District Court noted that the accused did not call any defence witnesses and did not address the court.

The trial judge at the Nicosia District Court noted that the accused had been told that they could cross-examine witnesses in turn and, if they so wished, choose one of their number to cross-examine the witnesses on behalf of all the accused, but that they had not done so.

Relying on the statements of the prosecution witnesses, the Nicosia District Court concluded that the accused had crossed the borders of the 'TRNC' at an unapproved entry point and without permission and had resisted by various means the UN and Turkish forces which had tried to stop them.
The Nicosia District Court found that the prosecution had proved its case beyond reasonable doubt and that the accused were guilty on both counts.

In deciding on the sentence, the Nicosia District Court took into account the seriousness of the offence and the fact that the accused had shown no remorse and continued to deny the validity of the 'TRNC'.
